cards.title: Drawing is seeing, not hand skill
cards.body: Your hand can already draw — the bottleneck is your eye. Learning to draw means learning to see: shapes, angles, gaps, and how light actually falls. Train observation first and the hand follows.

cards.title: Everything is spheres, boxes, and cylinders
cards.body: Construction: break any object into primitive 3D forms before adding detail. A head is a sphere plus a jaw wedge; an arm is a cylinder. Get the big forms right and the details almost place themselves.

The envelope trick: sketch a light bounding box (the 'envelope') around your whole subject first, then measure everything against it. If the head is half the envelope's height, your proportions are anchored before a single feature goes in.
Draw from the shoulder, not the wrist — big loose lines for big shapes. Warm up with two minutes of circles and straight lines; it loosens the arm and steadies everything after.

cards.q: What's the first thing to draw when starting any subject?
choices: The tiny details, to get them right
The outline in pen, no erasing
cards.explain: Construction first: block in spheres, boxes, and cylinders. Details on top of wrong forms just decorate the mistake.

flashcards.back: Building a drawing from simple 3D forms (spheres, boxes, cylinders) before adding detail.
The empty shapes around and between objects — drawing them helps you see proportions accurately.
A quick loose sketch capturing the action and flow of a pose, usually in under a minute.
Using the whole arm for big loose lines instead of cramped wrist movements.

questions.q: Why do beginners' drawings look 'off' even with careful lines?
choices: They draw symbols from memory instead of observing shapes
questions.explain: Most people draw their mental symbol of an eye or tree, not what's actually there. Observation beats hand control.

questions.q: A coffee mug is best constructed as…
choices: A cylinder plus a curved handle shape
questions.explain: Mug = cylinder body + handle loop. Construction turns 'hard objects' into easy primitives.
A bounding box around the subject locks in the big proportions first, so features land in the right place.

choices: The gaps between and around objects
questions.explain: The empty shapes between things are often easier to judge than the things themselves — use them as measuring tools.

choices: Two minutes of loose circles and lines
questions.explain: Loose warm-up lines wake up the shoulder and calm the 'first mark' nerves.

cards.title: Pick one light source and obey it
cards.body: Every shadow decision flows from a single question: where is the light? Mark it with a little sun in the corner of your page. The moment shadows disagree with each other, the drawing goes flat.

cards.title: The 5-value scale
cards.body: Highlight, light, midtone, core shadow, reflected light. That's the whole vocabulary of form. If you can render these five values on a sphere, you can render anything — faces, fabric, metal.

Shade a sphere in 4 steps: 1) outline the circle, 2) fill a flat midtone, 3) add the dark core shadow on the side away from the light, 4) leave the highlight untouched. The reflected light is the slight lift right at the shadow's edge.
Squint to see values. Squinting blurs detail and reveals the big light/dark shapes — if your drawing reads correctly while squinting, the values are right.

cards.q: What's the difference between core shadow and cast shadow?
choices: Core shadow is the dark side of the object itself; cast shadow is what it throws onto a surface
cards.explain: Core shadow lives ON the form (away from light); cast shadow is projected onto the ground or nearby surfaces.

flashcards.back: The darkest part of the object itself, on the side turned away from the light.
The shadow an object throws onto another surface.
Light bouncing off nearby surfaces back into the shadow side — a slight lift, never brighter than the light side.
How light or dark something is, independent of color — the backbone of realistic shading.

questions.q: The first rule of shading is…
choices: Decide where the single light source is
questions.explain: One light source, obeyed everywhere. Conflicting shadows flatten a drawing instantly.

choices: Highlight, light, midtone, core shadow, reflected light
questions.explain: Five values describe any form under light. Master them on a sphere and everything else follows.

choices: On the side facing the light
questions.explain: Highlight = the spot facing the light most directly. It's the brightest value and you preserve it by not shading there.
Squinting removes detail so you judge light vs dark masses — the structure shading depends on.

choices: As a slight lift inside the shadow edge
questions.explain: Bounced light lifts the shadow's edge slightly — it stays darker than anything on the lit side.

cards.title: The eyes sit halfway down the head
cards.body: Beginners put eyes near the top of the head. Reality: the eye line is at the halfway mark — the whole top half is forehead, hair, and skull. Measure it once and you'll never unsee it.

cards.title: The big three beginner mistakes
cards.body: Eyes too high, head too round (heads are longer than they are wide), and features drawn too big. Shrink the features, lengthen the skull, drop the eye line — faces instantly look more real.

The 30-second Loomis head: draw a ball, slice off the sides, attach a jaw wedge below, then cross the center lines (vertical for symmetry, horizontal for brow and nose). Every feature now has an address.
Ten bad drawings a day beats one precious one. Keep a cheap sketchbook you're not afraid to ruin — volume builds skill, perfectionism builds blank pages.

cards.q: Where does the eye line fall on a correctly proportioned head?
cards.explain: Eyes at the halfway line. The upper half is all cranium — that's why beginner faces look squished.

flashcards.back: Sits at the vertical halfway point of the head.
Ball + jaw wedge + center lines: a construction method giving every facial feature an address.
The head includes the cranium; the face (features) occupies roughly the bottom half.
Vertical line for symmetry, horizontal lines for brow/nose placement on a constructed head.

choices: Drawing eyes too high on the head
questions.explain: Eyes belong at the halfway line. Placing them higher is the single most common face error.
The cranium makes heads taller than wide. Round heads read as childlike or cartoonish.

questions.q: In the Loomis method, the jaw is…
choices: A wedge attached below the ball
questions.explain: Ball for the cranium, wedge for the jaw — then center lines place every feature.
Volume in a cheap sketchbook builds mileage. Precious paper makes you afraid to make the mistakes you learn from.

choices: Above the eye line, roughly a third of the way down from the crown
questions.explain: Brow sits above the eyes — roughly dividing the head into thirds: hairline, brow, nose-base, chin.
